static.topic: National Security Act, 1980 and Preventive Detention
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Article 22); Preventive Detention
static.whatIsIt: The NSA, 1980 is a preventive detention law that lets the Union or a State detain a person without charge or trial for up to 12 months, to prevent acts prejudicial to national security, public order or essential supplies and services.
static.background: Enacted in 1980, it followed earlier preventive detention regimes such as MISA, 1971 and the Defence of India Act, and was amended in 1984 and 1987. Under Article 22(4)–(7), detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board. Grounds of detention must ordinarily be communicated within five days, extendable to 15 days in exceptional circumstances with recorded reasons.
static.socioEconomic: Critics argue preventive detention is used disproportionately against activists, journalists and minorities; courts have repeatedly held that detention orders must rest on material and cannot become a tool to suppress dissent.
static.whyInNews: Assam activist Pranab Doley, who joined protests against a hotel near Kaziranga National Park, says an NSA case was filed against him to intimidate him and other land protesters.
static.wayForward: Stronger judicial review of detention orders, mandatory periodic review, and parliamentary scrutiny of how often and against whom the NSA is invoked.
prelimsPointers: The NSA permits detention without charge or trial for up to 12 months.
Detention beyond three months requires an Advisory Board's opinion.
Both the Union and State governments can invoke the NSA.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether preventive detention laws like the NSA are compatible with the constitutional scheme of fundamental rights and judicial review.

static.topic: Kaziranga National Park and Eco-Sensitive Zones
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Protected Areas, Conservation and Eco-Sensitive Zones
static.whatIsIt: Kaziranga National Park in Assam is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 1985) and a tiger reserve, best known for the greater one-horned rhinoceros. Eco-Sensitive Zones around protected areas are notified by the MoEFCC under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to regulate development in the immediate surroundings.
static.background: Kaziranga was declared a reserved forest in 1905, a game sanctuary in 1916, a wildlife sanctuary in 1950 and a national park in 1974; it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1985. It is also an Important Bird Area and a tiger reserve. ESZ notifications around Kaziranga have been revised and contested, with conservationists warning that a shrinking zone encourages unregulated construction.
static.geography: Spread along the Brahmaputra floodplain in Assam, the park is subject to annual flooding, and animals move through the adjoining Karbi Anglong hills.
static.socioEconomic: Tourism, hotels and road expansion around the park generate local livelihoods but also fragment habitat and block animal corridors; land disputes between park administration and local communities are long-standing.
static.whyInNews: Protests against a hotel coming up near Kaziranga led to an activist being booked under the NSA.
static.wayForward: Strict enforcement of ESZ rules, protection of animal corridors, participatory conservation with local communities, and transparent environmental clearances.
prelimsPointers: Kaziranga was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.
It is famous for the greater one-horned rhinoceros and is also a tiger reserve.
Eco-Sensitive Zones are notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the tension between tourism-led development around protected areas and the legal framework of eco-sensitive zones.

static.topic: Parliament, Legislation and Bills
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Parliament (Article 79) consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. A Bill becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent (Article 111).
static.background: Money Bills (Article 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can delay but not amend them on the money provisions. Ordinances (Article 123) can be promulgated when Parliament is not in session and must be approved within six weeks of reassembly. Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise Bills.
static.whyInNews: The NSA under which the Assam activist has been booked is a parliamentary statute; the episode renews questions about legislative scrutiny of laws that curtail personal liberty.
static.wayForward: Referral of liberty-affecting Bills to standing committees, periodic parliamentary review of preventive detention laws, and publication of data on detentions.
prelimsPointers: A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution differ in their effect on pending Bills.
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution of the Lok Sabha only if it has not yet been passed by the Lok Sabha.
static.mainsAngle: Assess declining legislative scrutiny and committee referrals; parliamentary productivity as a governance indicator.

prelims: The National Security Act, 1980 allows preventive detention without charge for up to 12 months; detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board's opinion.
Kaziranga National Park in Assam, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985, is known for the greater one-horned rhinoceros and is also a tiger reserve.

stories.mainsQuestion: Preventive detention laws are justified as necessary for public order, yet they sit uneasily with fundamental rights. Examine this tension in the context of protests against development projects near protected areas.

stories.headline: Noel Tata questions big-ticket investments as Tata group rift widens
stories.summary: Business Standard reports that Noel Tata, who chairs the Tata Trusts, has questioned the scale of large capital commitments being made across the Tata group, sharpening a disagreement over investment strategy inside the $185-billion conglomerate. The report frames the rift as deepening between the philanthropic trusts that control Tata Sons and the operating leadership pursuing big-ticket expansion. The dispute is described in terms of capital allocation and governance rather than any single transaction. Because the account rests on one business daily's reporting, the specifics of the disagreement are not independently corroborated here.
stories.whyItMatters: A promoter-level dispute over investment strategy is a live case study on holding-company control, board–shareholder power balances and how internal governance shapes India's private capex cycle — recurring GS-III territory.

perspectives.take: Frames it as a governance and capital-allocation rift at the very top of a $185-billion group, with the trusts' chair pushing back on aggressive investment plans; a business-press framing focused on corporate strategy and control.

static.topic: Tata Trusts–Tata Sons holding structure and promoter control
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Corporate Governance; Industrial Organisation and Business Structures
static.whatIsIt: Tata Sons is the unlisted principal holding company and promoter of the Tata group companies. A cluster of philanthropic endowments, collectively the Tata Trusts, holds a majority (roughly two-thirds) of Tata Sons' equity, which gives the trusts decisive control over the group even though they hold no direct stake in most operating companies.
static.background: The Tata endowment tradition dates to the group's founder, Jamsetji Tata, and the trusts created in the late 19th and early 20th centuries have historically held the dominant stake in Tata Sons. Ratan Tata chaired the trusts until his death in October 2024, after which Noel Tata was appointed chairman of Tata Trusts, while N. Chandrasekaran continued as chairman of Tata Sons. In 2016 the removal of Cyrus Mistry as chairman of Tata Sons triggered prolonged litigation, with the Supreme Court in 2021 upholding his removal.
static.geography: Mumbai, Maharashtra — Bombay House is the group headquarters.
static.socioEconomic: The group spans steel, automobiles, IT services, aviation and retail, and the trusts route a share of dividends into education, health and research philanthropy.
static.whyInNews: Reported pushback by the trusts' chair against large investment commitments by group companies, deepening an internal rift.
static.wayForward: Clearer disclosure norms for unlisted holding companies, formal capital-allocation review mechanisms and a transparent board–promoter interface would reduce the risk of such disputes spilling into public view.
prelimsPointers: Tata Sons is the promoter/holding company of Tata group firms and is itself unlisted.
Tata Trusts hold a majority stake in Tata Sons, so ultimate control of the group rests with the trusts.
The chairs of Tata Trusts and of Tata Sons are separate positions held by different individuals.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how promoter-holding company structures in Indian conglomerates affect corporate governance, minority shareholder interests and long-term capital allocation.

static.topic: Corporate governance framework for listed Indian companies
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Corporate Governance; Regulatory Bodies (SEBI, MCA, CCI)
static.whatIsIt: Listed companies must comply with the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations, 2015 — covering independent directors, audit and nomination committees, related-party transactions and periodic disclosure.
static.background: The Companies Act, 2013 replaced the 1956 Act and mandated independent directors, audit committees and CSR provisions. SEBI's LODR Regulations, 2015 consolidated listing obligations; the Kotak Committee (2017) recommended further board-governance reforms. The Competition Commission of India, under the Competition Act, 2002, separately vets combinations.
static.socioEconomic: Governance quality influences cost of capital, minority shareholder protection and overall investor confidence in Indian markets.
static.whyInNews: A promoter-level dispute over investment strategy in a large group renews attention on board independence and shareholder rights.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the effectiveness of independent directors, tighten related-party transaction approvals, and improve disclosure by unlisted holding entities that sit above listed companies.
prelimsPointers: SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 consolidated and replaced the earlier listing agreements.
The Companies Act, 2013 mandates independent directors and audit committees for prescribed classes of companies.
The CCI examines combinations under the Competition Act, 2002.
static.mainsAngle: Do India's corporate governance rules adequately protect minority shareholders in promoter-controlled conglomerates? Discuss with reference to recent disputes.

static.topic: Private capital expenditure and the investment cycle
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Investment, Growth and Industrial Policy
static.whatIsIt: Private capex — firms' spending on plant, machinery and new projects — is a key driver of growth, jobs and productivity, and responds to demand expectations, credit conditions and policy certainty.
static.background: India's investment cycle slowed after the twin balance-sheet stress of the 2010s, when bank NPAs constrained credit. In recent years public investment has led the recovery, with select large conglomerates announcing big commitments in semiconductors, green energy, aviation and digital infrastructure.
static.socioEconomic: Capex decisions affect employment, technology upgrading and regional industrial development.
static.whyInNews: An internal debate within a major conglomerate over the scale of big investments highlights how corporate governance shapes aggregate private capex.
static.wayForward: Policy certainty, access to long-term finance and speedy dispute resolution are needed to sustain private investment intentions.
prelimsPointers: Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) is the principal measure of investment in the national accounts.
Public capex has often preceded private capex in recent investment cycles.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the determinants of private capital expenditure in India and the role that governance within large conglomerates plays in shaping it.

prelims: Business Standard (November 2026) reported that Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, questioned large investment plans within the $185-billion Tata group.
Tata Sons is the unlisted holding company and promoter of Tata group companies; Tata Trusts are its majority shareholder.
The chairmanship of Tata Trusts and of Tata Sons are distinct positions — Noel Tata and N. Chandrasekaran respectively.
Promoter-holding structures concentrate control over listed operating companies without a proportionate direct equity stake.
stories.mainsQuestion: Promoter-controlled holding structures provide stability to large conglomerates but concentrate power in few hands. Critically examine this tension in the light of India's corporate governance reforms.

stories.headline: Violent protests in Hasina's hometown over proposed return from India
stories.summary: Violent protests broke out in Sheikh Hasina's hometown in Bangladesh over renewed talk of her returning from India, where she has lived since fleeing the country in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her government. The unrest signals how deeply the question of her return divides Bangladeshi politics and how quickly it can spill onto the street. For New Delhi, the episode sharpens a difficult balancing act: it hosts a former ally whom the current Bangladeshi authorities want to see face justice at home. The story is being carried by Indian outlets, with one of the two Hindu items being a syndicated duplicate of the same report; a third source in the feed covers an unrelated aviation accident in the United States.
stories.whyItMatters: India's handling of Sheikh Hasina's continued stay is now a live test of its Neighbourhood First policy, its extradition and asylum practice, and its ability to keep ties with Dhaka stable through a volatile political transition. It is a ready case study for questions on India's neighbourhood diplomacy and political instability in South Asia.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: India's bilateral relationship with Bangladesh, covering boundary settlement, water sharing, trade and connectivity, security cooperation and people-to-people ties. It is one of the most institutionally dense relationships India has with any neighbour, resting on a 1972 Treaty of Friendship, a land boundary settlement, a water-sharing treaty and an extradition treaty.
static.background: Bangladesh emerged as an independent state in 1971 with decisive Indian political, military and humanitarian support. The India–Bangladesh Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Peace was signed in 1972. The Land Boundary Agreement, agreed in 1974, was finally implemented in 2015 with a constitutional amendment enabling the exchange of enclaves and adversely possessed land. The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed in 1996. An extradition treaty between the two countries was signed in 2013. Relations have since been shaped by trade and transit connectivity, the Teesta water dispute, border management and periodic friction over migration and minority security.
static.geography: India and Bangladesh share a border of about 4,096.7 km — the longest India shares with any neighbour — touching West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Bangladesh sits on the Bay of Bengal and shares the Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta system with India.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is a major destination for Indian exports and a source of readymade garment imports; Indian transit and connectivity projects (BBIN, Chattogram and Mongla port access) are central to the relationship. Cross-border migration, informal trade and minority welfare remain sensitive social issues on both sides.
static.whyInNews: Violent protests erupted in Sheikh Hasina's hometown over renewed tensions around her proposed return to Bangladesh from India, where she has stayed since August 2024.
static.wayForward: India needs to keep channels open with Dhaka's current authorities while managing the politically charged question of Hasina's presence, and to insulate long-term cooperation — water, trade, connectivity, border management — from short-term political turbulence.
prelimsPointers: India shares its longest land border with Bangladesh — about 4,096.7 km.
The Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh was implemented in 2015 through a constitutional amendment.
Bangladesh is a member of SAARC, BIMSTEC, the Bay of Bengal Initiative grouping and the Commonwealth.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how political instability in Bangladesh tests India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest how India can de-risk its core interests from regime-level volatility.

static.topic: Bangladesh's Post-2024 Political Transition
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Political Developments in India's Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The political reordering of Bangladesh after the student-led uprising of July–August 2024 forced Sheikh Hasina from office, leading to an interim government and a contested transitional justice process.
static.background: The 2024 unrest began as a student movement against the reservation quota in public employment and escalated into a nationwide anti-government agitation. Sheikh Hasina resigned and left the country in August 2024, taking refuge in India. An interim government headed by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus assumed office and promised institutional reform and accountability for the crackdown. Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal has since been conducting proceedings relating to the July 2024 violence, and the political landscape remains polarised between the Awami League's support base and the parties that led the agitation.
static.geography: Bangladesh is a South Asian state on the Bay of Bengal, bordered by India on three sides and by Myanmar on the south-east, and is one of the world's most densely populated large countries.
static.socioEconomic: The economy depends heavily on readymade garment exports and remittances, making it sensitive to political disruption, currency pressure and investor confidence. Youth unemployment and inflation were among the underlying grievances behind the 2024 protests.
static.whyInNews: Protests turned violent in Sheikh Hasina's hometown amid rising tensions over her proposed return from India.
static.wayForward: A durable settlement requires an inclusive political process, credible and non-selective accountability, and an electoral roadmap that all major parties accept; external partners can support stability but cannot substitute for domestic consensus.
prelimsPointers: Sheikh Hasina left Bangladesh in August 2024 following a student-led uprising and has since been in India.
An interim government headed by Muhammad Yunus took charge in Bangladesh after her departure.
Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal handles cases relating to crimes against humanity and the July 2024 crackdown.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how regime change in a neighbouring state reshapes bilateral relations, using Bangladesh's post-2024 transition to illustrate the limits and possibilities of India's neighbourhood diplomacy.

static.topic: Extradition and Asylum in International Law
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Law: Extradition and Asylum
static.whatIsIt: Extradition is the formal surrender of an accused or convicted person by one state to another for trial or punishment, governed by bilateral treaties or domestic law. Asylum is the protection a state grants to a foreign national on its territory, which can conflict with a requesting state's extradition demand.
static.background: There is no single global extradition regime; obligations arise from bilateral treaties and domestic statutes such as India's Extradition Act, 1962. India has extradition treaties with a large number of countries, including Bangladesh, with which a treaty was signed in 2013. Standard safeguards include the dual criminality requirement, the political offence exception, and the rule of speciality. Asylum and non-refoulement obligations derive principally from international human rights and refugee law instruments, to which India is not a full treaty party.
static.whyInNews: Sheikh Hasina's continued presence in India, and Bangladeshi demands for her return, have revived questions about how India reconciles treaty-based extradition obligations with political and humanitarian considerations.
static.wayForward: India should handle such requests through a transparent, legally grounded process that weighs treaty obligations, domestic law and diplomatic consequences, while pressing for a broader bilateral framework on judicial cooperation.
prelimsPointers: India's law on extradition is the Extradition Act, 1962; obligations flow mainly from bilateral treaties.
Dual criminality — the act must be an offence in both states — is a standard condition for extradition.
India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the tension between a state's extradition obligations under bilateral treaties and the political and humanitarian considerations that shape its response to requests concerning former heads of government.

prelims: Sheikh Hasina fled Bangladesh in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her government and has since been staying in India.
India shares about 4,096.7 km of border with Bangladesh — the longest India shares with any neighbour.
India and Bangladesh signed an extradition treaty in 2013; India's domestic extradition law is the Extradition Act, 1962.
Bangladesh is a member of SAARC, BIMSTEC and the Commonwealth, and its interim government is headed by Muhammad Yunus.
stories.mainsQuestion: Political instability in Bangladesh has repeatedly tested India's Neighbourhood First approach. Analyse the diplomatic, legal and security dilemmas that the continued presence of Sheikh Hasina in India poses for New Delhi, and suggest a principled framework for managing such situations with neighbouring states.

stories.headline: ASEAN leaders denounce Myanmar violence, extend ban on its military chief
stories.summary: Southeast Asian leaders, meeting at an ASEAN summit, publicly denounced the continuing violence in Myanmar and extended the restriction barring the country's military leader from the grouping's top-level meetings. The move continues a position ASEAN has held since 2021, when it first limited Myanmar's representation after the army seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government. The stated framework remains the Five-Point Consensus, which ASEAN leaders proposed in April 2021 to try to ease the violence and open dialogue among all parties. Progress on that plan has been minimal, and ASEAN's norms of consensus and non-interference leave it with few enforcement tools. The decision keeps Myanmar's crisis on the regional agenda while signalling that the bloc will not confer full legitimacy on the junta at summit level.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests ASEAN's credibility and 'centrality' in regional security, and directly bears on India's Act East policy, its long land border with Myanmar, and refugee and security spillovers into the Northeast.

perspectives.take: Frames the development as a diplomatic rebuke by Southeast Asian leaders, anchoring it to the April 2021 plan devised after the army seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government; a wire-style international report with limited India-specific analysis.

static.topic: ASEAN and the Myanmar Question
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Regional Groupings and Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: ASEAN is a ten-member regional organisation of Southeast Asian states coordinating political-security, economic and socio-cultural cooperation. It anchors several Asia-Pacific institutions and has led regional diplomacy on Myanmar since the 2021 coup.
static.background: Founded on 8 August 1967 in Bangkok through the ASEAN (Bangkok) Declaration by Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Brunei joined in 1984, Vietnam in 1995, Laos and Myanmar in 1997, and Cambodia in 1999. The ASEAN Charter, adopted in 2007 and in force from 2008, gave the grouping legal personality and codified the 'ASEAN Way' — consensus decision-making and non-interference in members' internal affairs. The Secretariat is in Jakarta.
static.geography: Southeast Asia, spanning the Indochina mainland and the Malay and Philippine archipelagos; the Strait of Malacca, Sunda and Lombok are strategic sea-lane chokepoints.
static.socioEconomic: A market of over 600 million people and one of the world's largest combined economies; RCEP, in force since 2022, links ASEAN with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. India is a dialogue partner and participates in the East Asia Summit and ASEAN Regional Forum.
static.whyInNews: ASEAN leaders denounced violence in Myanmar and extended the ban on its leader attending top-level ASEAN meetings.
static.wayForward: Deepen India-ASEAN connectivity and supply-chain links while pressing for a credible ASEAN envoy mechanism on Myanmar; balance ASEAN centrality against India's own border and refugee concerns.
prelimsPointers: ASEAN was founded on 8 August 1967 in Bangkok by five states; it now has ten members.
Myanmar joined ASEAN in 1997; the ASEAN Secretariat is in Jakarta.
Decisions are taken by consensus, with non-interference in internal affairs as a core principle.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether ASEAN's consensus-based, non-interference model can deliver on regional security crises such as Myanmar, and what this implies for India's Act East policy.

static.topic: Myanmar Crisis and the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood; Regional Groupings
static.whatIsIt: The Five-Point Consensus is ASEAN's April 2021 plan for Myanmar: immediate cessation of violence and restraint by all parties; constructive dialogue among all parties; appointment of an ASEAN special envoy to facilitate mediation; humanitarian assistance through the AHA Centre; and a special envoy visit to meet all concerned parties.
static.background: Myanmar's military (Tatmadaw) seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining Aung San Suu Kyi and President Win Myint after the National League for Democracy's victory in the November 2020 elections. ASEAN leaders met in Jakarta in April 2021 and adopted the Five-Point Consensus with Senior General Min Aung Hlaing present. Since October 2021, ASEAN has restricted Myanmar's representation at summits to a non-political level.
static.geography: Myanmar borders India (Mizoram, Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh), Bangladesh, China, Laos and Thailand, and has a long coastline on the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea.
static.socioEconomic: Conflict has pushed refugees and displaced persons towards the Indian border, especially Mizoram; it disrupts India's Kaladan multi-modal transit project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, and feeds cross-border trafficking and arms flows.
static.whyInNews: ASEAN leaders again denounced violence in Myanmar and extended the exclusion of its leader from summit-level meetings, with the Five-Point Consensus still the stated framework.
static.wayForward: A credible, unified ASEAN envoy with access to all parties; humanitarian corridors through the AHA Centre; and for India, calibrated engagement that protects border stability and connectivity projects without conferring legitimacy on the junta.
prelimsPointers: The Five-Point Consensus was adopted at the ASEAN Leaders' Meeting in Jakarta in April 2021.
Myanmar's military seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining Aung San Suu Kyi.
The AHA Centre is ASEAN's humanitarian coordination body, based in Jakarta.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why the Five-Point Consensus has stalled and examine its implications for India's border management, connectivity projects and Act East policy.

static.topic: UN Security Council, R2P and Myanmar
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and Multilateral Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN, founded in 1945, has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. The Responsibility to Protect (R2P), endorsed at the 2005 World Summit, holds states responsible for protecting populations from atrocity crimes.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for permanent Security Council seats, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on reform remain inconclusive. Action on Myanmar at the UNSC has repeatedly been constrained by vetoes or the threat of vetoes.
static.whyInNews: ASEAN's rebuke of Myanmar's military leadership highlights the limits of regional diplomacy and renews questions about UNSC paralysis and the application of R2P in cases of internal repression.
static.wayForward: Push for an expanded, more representative UNSC and for R2P to be applied consistently rather than selectively; strengthen regional organisations as complementary pillars of conflict prevention.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent and 10 elected for two-year terms.
The ICJ sits at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
R2P was endorsed at the 2005 UN World Summit.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions; assess the obstacles, including veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

prelims: ASEAN was set up by the Bangkok Declaration on 8 August 1967; it has ten members and its Secretariat is in Jakarta.
The Five-Point Consensus on Myanmar was adopted at the ASEAN Leaders' Meeting in Jakarta in April 2021.
Myanmar's military seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining Aung San Suu Kyi; ASEAN has restricted Myanmar's summit representation since October 2021.

stories.mainsQuestion: ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus has not ended the crisis in Myanmar. Examine the structural constraints on ASEAN's conflict-resolution role and discuss the implications for India's Act East policy and border management.

stories.headline: China pushes AI literacy into classrooms to raise an AI-native generation
stories.summary: Reports carried by Reuters and republished by other outlets describe a concerted Chinese effort to make AI literacy a routine part of schooling, so that students grow up using and building with AI tools rather than meeting them only at university or in the workplace. The drive is presented as part of Beijing's broader ambition to convert its large education system into a pipeline of AI-capable talent, spanning curriculum changes, teacher training and classroom tools. The coverage is essentially a single wire story reproduced across outlets, so it offers a broad sketch rather than detailed policy specifics or independent verification. It situates China's approach within a wider global contest over AI capability, in which education systems are treated as strategic infrastructure rather than a purely social service.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-III (Science & Technology, indigenisation, employment) and GS-II (education, governance, India's response to global technological competition). Useful for questions on AI skilling, curriculum reform and the future of work.

perspectives.take: The original wire report frames China's classroom AI push as a deliberate, state-led generational bet; neutral, global wire perspective with no independent verification of specifics.

stories.headline: US FAA to audit India's aviation safety oversight as DGCA braces for review
stories.summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) will begin an audit of India's aviation safety oversight from Monday, examining how the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) licenses personnel, certifies operators and conducts surveillance and enforcement. The review is taking place even as India retains Category 1 status under the FAA's International Aviation Safety Assessment (IASA) programme, which permits Indian carriers to operate services to the United States and enter code-share arrangements with US airlines. The assessment targets the regulator's systems rather than the safety record of any individual carrier, but its findings carry commercial weight at a time when Indian airlines are expanding international routes and fleet orders. The outcome could also influence reciprocal recognition of Indian certifications by other foreign regulators.
stories.whyItMatters: Aviation safety oversight is now a determinant of market access, so the audit tests India's regulatory capacity in a sector central to services trade and connectivity. It links GS-III infrastructure questions with GS-II issues of international standard-setting and regulatory governance.

perspectives.take: Straight, wire-style framing that foregrounds the event itself — the FAA auditing India's safety oversight standards — with neutral, non-alarmist tone.
Sector-specialist framing that leads with the operational detail of the audit starting Monday, treating it as routine regulatory business rather than a crisis for Indian aviation.
Anchors the report in India's Category 1 status, implicitly reassuring readers that US-bound operations and code-shares are not immediately at risk.

static.topic: DGCA and Civil Aviation Safety Oversight in India
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure — Civil Aviation; Statutory and Regulatory Bodies
static.whatIsIt: The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), under the Ministry of Civil Aviation, is India's civil aviation safety regulator. It licenses pilots, engineers and other personnel, certifies airworthiness and air operators, and conducts surveillance of airlines and airports. It draws powers from the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the Aircraft Rules, 1937, and works alongside the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (security) and the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (investigation).
static.background: Civil aviation regulation in India traces back to the Aircraft Act, 1934. The DGCA has long functioned as an attached office of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and a proposal to replace it with an independent statutory Civil Aviation Authority has been discussed but not enacted. India was downgraded by the FAA to Category 2 in 2014 over deficiencies in safety oversight and restored to Category 1 in 2018 after a series of DGCA reforms.
static.geography: India's aviation system is anchored in major hubs such as Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, with international gateways relevant to long-haul US-bound routes.
static.socioEconomic: Civil aviation supports tourism, trade in services and high-skill employment; a regulator's international standing affects airline expansion plans, connectivity and fares.
static.whyInNews: An FAA team is to audit the DGCA's safety oversight systems from Monday while India holds Category 1 status.
static.wayForward: Strengthen DGCA manpower and technical specialisation, move towards an independent statutory aviation authority, and institutionalise data-driven surveillance and safety management systems across operators.
prelimsPointers: India currently holds FAA Category 1 status under the International Aviation Safety Assessment (IASA) programme.
Category 1 status allows Indian carriers to operate to the US and enter code-share arrangements with US airlines.
The DGCA is India's civil aviation safety regulator under the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's civil aviation regulator has the institutional capacity to keep pace with the sector's growth, and suggest reforms to align oversight with global benchmarks.

static.topic: ICAO, FAA IASA and Global Aviation Safety Oversight
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Institutions and Standard-Setting
static.whatIsIt: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), a UN specialised agency created by the 1944 Chicago Convention, sets global standards and recommended practices (Annexes) for safety, security and navigation, and audits member states through the Universal Safety Oversight Audit Programme (USOAP). Separately, the US FAA's IASA programme assesses whether a foreign state's safety oversight of its airlines meets ICAO standards, assigning Category 1 or Category 2.
static.background: The Chicago Convention of 1944 established ICAO, headquartered in Montreal. Article 33 of the Convention concerns recognition of certificates and licences issued by other states, and Article 37 concerns adoption of international standards — the legal basis for mutual recognition that makes such audits consequential for airlines' foreign operations.
static.geography: ICAO is headquartered in Montreal, Canada; the FAA is headquartered in Washington, D.C.
static.socioEconomic: Assessment outcomes affect market access, code-share permissions and the ability of carriers to expand into long-haul international markets.
static.whyInNews: The FAA audit of India's oversight revives focus on how foreign regulators assess national safety systems and on the standards that underpin mutual recognition.
static.wayForward: Deepen compliance with ICAO Annexes, publish safety performance data transparently, and pursue mutual recognition arrangements to reduce duplicative audits.
prelimsPointers: ICAO, established in 1944 by the Chicago Convention, is headquartered in Montreal.
The FAA's IASA classifies countries as Category 1 (meets ICAO standards) or Category 2 (does not).
USOAP is ICAO's audit programme for member states' safety oversight capabilities.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how international standard-setting bodies shape domestic regulatory reform, using civil aviation safety oversight as an illustration.

prelims: The US FAA will audit India's aviation safety oversight from Monday.
India holds Category 1 status under the FAA's IASA programme, which permits Indian carriers to fly to the US.
The audit examines the DGCA's oversight systems, not the safety record of any single airline.
FAA IASA assessments are distinct from ICAO's USOAP audits of member states.
